Serbia’s government has formally terminated Jared Kushner’s controversial plan for a $500 million Trump-branded luxury complex in the country’s capital city, Belgrade.

According to TVP World, an English-language news outlet based in Poland, Serbia’s Ministry of Construction confirmed that the official process for a termination agreement was expected to be completed this week.

Construction Minister Aleksandra Sofronijević said the Serbian government decided in August to end its deal with Kushner, who is President Donald Trump’s son-in-law.

In December, The Wall Street Journal broke the news that Kushner’s investment firm, Affinity Partners, was abandoning the project, which would have included a high-rise hotel, offices, shops and residential units.

“Our vision for the Belgrade project was to offer an elegant, uplifting design that honored Serbia’s progress. We are proud of the architecture our team created,” an Affinity Partners spokesperson told Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty in a statement last December.

“Because meaningful projects should unite rather than divide, and out of respect for the people of Serbia and the City of Belgrade, we are withdrawing our application and stepping aside at this time,” the statement continued.

Much of the controversy surrounding the Belgrade project stemmed from its location. The complex was designed for a site that previously served as the Yugoslav Ministry of Defense headquarters, which was heavily damaged in a 1999 NATO bombing campaign meant to halt ethnic cleansing led by Serbian President Slobodan Milošević.

As The Wall Street Journal pointed out, the site is presently a ruin but remains a prime example of mid-20th century architecture and a symbol of national identity to many Serbians. The government’s contract with Affinity Partners included a provision to strip the site of its cultural heritage designation before construction began.

The news drew massive protests across Belgrade that intensified when Serbian Culture Minister Nikola Selakovic was arrested for allegedly forging documents to hasten the process of removing the site’s protected status.

Affinity Partners’ now-defunct proposal for the Belgrade complex preceded its plan for a $1.6 billion resort in Albania, to be located on a stretch of the Adriatic coast.

In June, that project also drew massive protests, with Albanian environmentalists arguing that its construction would disrupt wetlands that serve as nesting sites for flamingos, seals and sea turtles, among other animals.
